Petitioner, OAL DKT. NO.: TYP 11798-07
v.
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT
SYSTEM,
Respondent.
__________________________________
Jonathan S. Fabricant, Esq., for petitioner (Bathgate, Wegener and Wolf,
attorneys)
Danielle Bradus, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (Anne Milgram,
Attorney General of New Jersey, attorney)
Record Returned to OAL September 9, 2009 Decided: September 22, 2009
BEFORE CAROL I. COHEN, ALJ:
PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The petitioner, Cynthia Wesley, filed an Application for Disability Retirement on February 1, 2007. In June 20, 2007, the Board of Trustees of the
Public Employees' Retirement System (PERS) denied the petitioner's application. The Board found that Ms. Wesley was not totally and
permanently disabled from the performance of her regular and assigned duties. However, with her age and/or years of service, she qualified for a
deferred retirement. On July 19, 2007, the petitioner, through counsel, sent a letter to the Secretary of the Board requesting that the matter be
referred to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) for a hearing. The Board approved the petitioner's request for an administrative hearing on
August 15, 2007.
The matter was filed with the OAL on November 13, 2007. A telephone pre-hearing conference was held on December 26, 2007. The matter
was originally scheduled for a hearing on July 16 and 17, 2008. The case was adjourned because the petitioner's expert had recently undergone
hip surgery. It was rescheduled for February 4 and 19, 2009. The February 4 date was adjourned because of the Judge's scheduling conflict. That
date was rescheduled to March 2, 2009. The matter was heard on February 19. However, the March date had to be adjourned because one of
the petitioner's expert witnesses was not available to testify. The matter was rescheduled for May 8, 2009, and heard on that date. Summation
briefs were received on July 6, 2009. An initial decision was issued on July 29, 2009. The PERS Board filed exceptions on August 11, 2009. On
August 20, 2009 the Board remanded the matter back to the ALJ for clarification as to whether the petitioner was totally and permanently
disabled from employment as of the date of her retirement. On September 17, 2009 I had a telephone conference with the attorneys for the
parties. They both agreed that no further submissions were necessary and my decision should be made by a review of the prior record.
ISSUE
Whether the petitioner was totally and permanently disabled from employment as of the date of her retirement?
FINDINGS OF FACT
See prior findings in July 29, 2009 Initial Decision

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The applicable statute that governs the case of Ordinary Disability states:
A member, under 60 years of age, who has 10 or more years of credit for New Jersey service, shall, upon the
application of the head of the department in which he shall have been employed or upon his own application or the
application of one acting in his behalf, be retired for ordinary disability by the board of trustees. The physician or
physicians designated by the board shall have first made a medical examination of him at his residence or at any
other place mutually agreed upon and shall have certified to the board that the member is physically or mentally
incapacitated for the performance of duty and should be retired.
[N.J.S.A. 43:15A-42 (emphasis added).]
In their exceptions the Board argued that:
Dr. Klemons testified that he discharged Petitioner asymptomatic from his care in December 2006, and could not
state whether or not Petitioner was disabled at that time. In July 2008, when Petitioner returned to Dr. Klemons, he
concluded that Petitioner was totally and permanently [disabled] from general secretarial work based on his
examination. This determination was made over a year after Petitioner applied for an ordinary disability retirement
in 2007 and long after Petitioner stopped working in January 2006.
Similarly, Dr. Othee, Petitioner's pain management specialist, testified that Petitioner left his care in February 2007,
even though he recommended a follow-up appointment in four weeks…..It is at this point, in July 2008, that Dr.
Othee opined that Petitioner is totally and permanently disabled. Thus, based on the competent, credible evidence
in the record, including the testimony of Petitioner's medical experts, Petitioner was not totally and permanently
disabled until July 2008.
I do not concur with the argument put forward by the Board. While it is true that in Dr. Klemons initial report he discharged the petitioner as
asymptomatic, he also made it clear in his testimony that it did not mean that the problem did not persist.
Dr. Klemons recounted that Mrs. Wesley Jackson first came to him on August 23, 2006, complaining of eye pain, blurred vision, pressure
in the ears, ear aches, jaw pain and fatigue, clicking sounds in her jaw, pain when chewing and yawning, sinus pain, dryness in the mouth, pain in
her teeth, shoulder, hand and back. . His working diagnosis of her condition was that she had experienced stretching and tearing in the mandibular
area with spasm and degenerative changes in the face, head and shoulders. She was experiencing headaches and facial pain, myositis, swallow
dysphasia, inflammatory arthritis, temporal tendonitis, limited mandibular range of motion. In addition the disc of the TMJ was dislocated and there
were joint changes as a result of trauma. It was Dr. Klemons opinion that the symptoms that Mrs. Wesley Jackson was experiencing were, to a
reasonable degree of medical probability, the result of the trauma that she had sustained in the automobile accident.
Dr. Klemons stated that he treated the petitioner until December 8, 2006, when she moved to Virginia. When asked about the limitations
that she claimed that she experienced as a result of the condition, he said that she stated that she had difficulty cleaning, standing, kneeling in
church, chewing gum and kissing. It also interfered with her ability to participate in sports and have normal sexual relations. She spent a lot of time
in bed and she felt extremely stressed. Dr. Klemons opined that these symptoms were consistent with the type of injuries that she had sustained.
His working diagnosis was that she had muscle stretching and tearing with spasm and degenerative changes in the face, head and shoulders. She
suffered from myalgia, headaches and facial pain, myositis, swallow dysphasia, inflammatory arthritis, temporal tendonitis, thoracic outlet
syndrome, limited mandibular range of motion, dislocation of the disc of the TMJ and joint changes as a result of trauma.
At the time that Mrs. Wesley Jackson moved to Virginia, Dr. Klemons had hoped that she would be able to maintain the improved
condition that he had seen prior to her leaving. He recommended that she try to wean herself from the device he had made for her. When she
attempted to do so her condition worsened as he reported when he saw her on July 15, 2008. Further, when he was queried about what had
changed between 2006 when he had discharged Mrs. Wesley Jackson from treatment as asymptomatic and now when he was stating that she was
permanently disabled, he testified that what had happened was that time had taken its toll. He might have been able to reduce her pain but her
problem i.e., muscle damage, spasm and degenerative changes to muscles, ligaments, tendons and joints of the head, face, neck and shoulders
persisted. The medications that she was taking masked her pain somewhat, but did not resolve the underlying condition.
Looking at Dr. Klemon's testimony in its totality it is clear that while Ms. Wesley Jackson's condition improved for a short period of time it was a
temporary cessation of a continuing deterioration caused by the motor vehicle accident. Her disabling condition continued to exist.
Dr. Othee, who testified as Mrs. Wesley Jackson's treating pain management physician, diagnosed her as having a chronic S-1 radiculopathy in her
low back causing pain and numbness in her back and neck and numbness and tingling down her right arm. He also noted reduced range of motion.
He testified that he had performed a number of diagnostic tests including an EMG to try to determine the cause of her pain. He stated that the
objective tests that he performed validated the subjective complaints that Mrs. Wesley Jackson had reported to him. On October 19, 2006, Mrs.
Wesley Jackson reported that her low-back pain was improved, but her range of motion was restricted and she was positive for leg raises on her
right side. Dr. Othee recommended a continuation of physical therapy and motrin for pain. In subsequent visits the petitioner reported an increase
in pain and Dr.Othee prescribed medication to alleviate the pain and muscle spasms. He continued to recommend that she not return to work
because of her pain and the side effects, including drowsiness caused by the medications that she was taking. When she returned on December 16,
2006 Mrs. Wesley Jackson reported no change in her level of pain. Similarly on January 11, 2007, she reported no change. The doctor

recommended continuing physical therapy and gave her lydoderm patches to manage her pain. There seem to have been no change in her level of
pain when she came to see Dr. Othee on February 15, 2007. Thus, at the time Mrs. Wesley Jackson filed her application for retirement, she was
suffering the same symptoms that she continued to report to Dr. Othee. While her condition continued to deteriorate, as Dr. Othee reported when
he saw her in July 2008, about sixteen months later, it is clear that the same problem, that had caused Dr. Othee to recommend that she continue in
treatment and not return to work, had persisted. Even though she sought medical treatment when she moved to Virginia, her condition did not
improve, in fact it became worse. Dr. Othee viewed her symptoms as being chronic and recommended that she not sit, bend, stand or walk for
prolonged periods of time. This was a continuation of his recommendation from 2006 and 2007, when he ordered that she not return to work,
because she could not perform the normal duties of a secretary.
CONCLUSION
Based on the above findings of fact and analysis of the law, I CONCLUDE that the petitioner was permanently disabled from the
performance of her duties at the time she initially filed for retirement benefits on February 1, 2007 and is therefore entitled to ordinary disability
benefits from that date forward.
ORDER
It is hereby ORDERED that the petitioner's application for disability retirement benefits is hereby GRANTED effective February 1,
2007.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM for
consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES'
RETIREMENT SYSTEM, which by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees'
Retirement System does not adopt, modify or reject this decision within forty-five days and unless such time limit is otherwise extended, this
recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
Within thirteen days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written exceptions with the
DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF PENSIONS, One State Street Square, 50 West State Street, P.O. Box 295, Trenton, New Jersey
08625-0295, marked "Attention: Exceptions." A copy of any exceptions must be sent to the judge and to the other parties.
